introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0750), Paper 2, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2026. Duration: THREE HOURS.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section.

All questions carry TWENTY-FIVE marks each. You are encouraged to refer to specific examples drawn from any part of the world. Credit will be given for such specific examples.

Only the required number of questions will be marked.

Marks will be awarded for well annotated maps and diagrams where these are relevant.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « Answer FOUR questions, choosing at least ONE from each Section » (Section A : questions 1 à 3, Section B : questions 4 à 6, Section C : question 7 seule). `regles_choix` porte le minimum imposé par section (`parmi 1 sur 3` pour A et B, `parmi 1 sur 1` pour C) ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`. La question 7 offre deux versions (EITHER / OR) : sous-questions codées « a », « b » (EITHER) et « OR-a », « OR-b » (OR), reliées par une règle `ou` (deux sous-questions « a » dans un même exercice seraient refusées).

Question 5(a)(ii) : le sujet laisse le choix entre deux questions (EITHER industries « foot loose » / OR couloirs maritimes), chacune de 7 marks, à l'intérieur de la sous-question « a » (16 points : (i) 9 + (ii) 7). La règle `ou` s'applique à tout un groupe de sections et ne peut donc pas l'exprimer sans fausser les questions 4 et 6 ; le corrigé traite les deux versions de (ii), signalées « EITHER » et « OR (alternative question) ».

Points : chaque question est imprimée à 25 marks et les sous-parties somment bien à 25 (Q1 6+4+4+6+5 ; Q2 8+8+9 ; Q3 8+9+8 ; Q4 9+9+7 ; Q5 9+7+9 ; Q6 4+6+6+9 ; Q7 EITHER 15+10, OR 5+5+9+6). Les sous-questions regroupant des parties (i) et (ii) (1a, 1b, 5a, 6a, OR-a, OR-b) portent la somme de leurs marks (10, 10, 16, 10, 10, 15) ; les marks de chaque partie restent imprimés dans l'énoncé. Aucun écart avec le sujet.

Défauts d'impression du sujet, transcrits avec le minimum de retouches : Q1(a) « heavy or less precipitation » (formulation maladroite, recopiée) ; Q2(a) se termine par deux points (« surface.. »), un seul conservé ; Q4 « The unven distribution » (faute d'impression pour « uneven », corrigée dans la transcription) ; Q4(c) se termine par une virgule (« sparsely populated, ») ; Q5(a)(ii) une apostrophe parasite devant « Discuss » (non recopiée) ; Q5(a)(ii) OR et Q5(b) se terminent par un point d'interrogation alors que la phrase est une consigne (« Explain... ? », « Explain THREE efforts... sector? »), recopié tel quel ; Q7 la version OR n'est pas numérotée (« OR » puis a), b)) et les parties (i) et (ii) du b) de la version OR sont numérotées « i) » et « ii) » sous « b) ». La page 3 du scan montre en marge gauche des fragments de caractères sans lien avec le sujet, ignorés.

Sujet scanné de trois pages (page de garde, deux pages de questions), filigranes et bandeaux gcerevision.com sans incidence sur la lecture, ignorés. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Geography 2, Paper 2, code 0750, JUNE 2026, THREE HOURS, référence GCE26/0750/2/P52. Aucune carte, aucun graphique ni document imprimé dans ce sujet : aucune figure d'énoncé ; les trois figures déclarées (profil de sol, courbes de Malthus et de Boserup, rente économique de Von Thünen) sont des schémas qualitatifs produits pour les corrigés (origine « corrige »), non à l'échelle, sans valeur numérique.

Les exemples cités (lieux, programmes, accords, institutions) sont des exemples reconnus ; les chiffres sont des ordres de grandeur donnés avec « about », « roughly » ou « more than ». Le point sur l'insécurité récente (régions du Sud-Ouest et du Nord-Ouest) est un fait contemporain cité avec prudence.

Question 5(b) : les actions de l'État cité (barrage de Lom Pangar, Memve'ele, centrale à gaz de Kribi, projet de Nachtigal, port en eau profonde de Kribi, régime des zones franches depuis le début des années 1990, Charte des investissements de 2002, Cameroon Business Forum, stratégies DSCE et SND 2020-2030) sont des faits reconnus mais l'état d'avancement actuel de chaque projet (en particulier Nachtigal) et les dates exactes sont à vérifier. Question 6(c) : taux d'urbanisation « d'environ 55 à 60 pour cent » = estimation récente, ordre de grandeur.

Question 7(a) : exemples cités (crues de printemps de la Red River en 1997, tsunami de décembre 2004 avec plus de 200 000 morts, tsunami du Tohoku en 2011, crues du Yangtsé en 1998 en partie attribuées à la déforestation, inondations de Douala et de Yaoundé) reconnus mais à faire relire ; le rôle de la déforestation dans les crues du Yangtsé reste discuté.

questions.enonce_markdown:
a) People in some parts of the world suffer the effects of heavy or less precipitation.

i) Why is the rate of precipitation not uniform on the Earth's surface?

(6 marks)

ii) Examine the principal characteristics of Mountain Climates.

(4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Why the rate of precipitation is not uniform (6 marks)**

Precipitation needs air that rises, cools to its dew point, condenses and forms droplets or ice crystals heavy enough to fall. Any factor that changes how much moisture the air holds, or how easily it is forced to rise, makes the rate of precipitation vary from place to place. The main factors are the following (a candidate should explain at least three or four of them, with examples).

1. **Latitude and the pressure belts.** Near the Equator the strong heating produces intense **convection**, and the trade winds converge in the **ITCZ** (low pressure, rising moist air), so rainfall is heavy (the Congo Basin, the Amazon Basin, southern Cameroon). Around 20 to 30 degrees north and south, air **descends** in the subtropical high-pressure belts, warms and dries, so these areas are mainly hot deserts (the Sahara, the Kalahari, central Australia). In the mid-latitudes (about 40 to 60 degrees) **fronts and depressions** bring frequent rain (north-west Europe). Near the poles the air is very cold, holds little water vapour and precipitation is low.
2. **Distance from the sea (continentality).** Places near the sea receive moist maritime air and have more rain; the interiors of large continents are far from the moisture source and are drier (the Gobi Desert in central Asia, the interior of Australia).
3. **Relief.** Air forced up a mountain cools and gives **orographic (relief) rainfall** on the windward slope; the leeward side lies in a **rain shadow** and is dry because the descending air warms. Example: the windward Atlantic side of Mount Cameroon is among the wettest places in Africa, while the Western Ghats of India are very wet and the Deccan plateau behind them is drier.
4. **Ocean currents.** Warm currents (the North Atlantic Drift) warm the air and increase evaporation and rainfall on the adjoining coast. **Cold currents** (Benguela, Humboldt or Peru, Canary) cool and stabilise the air, so coasts beside them are very dry: the Namib and Atacama deserts.
5. **Prevailing winds and air masses.** Onshore winds (the south-west monsoon in West Africa and Cameroon) bring moisture; offshore continental winds (the dry, dusty Harmattan from the Sahara) bring none, which explains the long dry season of northern Cameroon.
6. **Local factors.** Altitude, the amount of vegetation (forests add moisture through evapotranspiration) and large towns (heat-island effect) can slightly increase or reduce local rainfall.

**Conclusion.** Precipitation is therefore a product of the interaction of latitude, distance from the sea, relief, currents and winds, and no two places receive exactly the same amount.

**(ii) Principal characteristics of mountain climates (4 marks)**

Mountain (highland) climates differ from those of the surrounding lowlands at the same latitude, mainly because of **altitude**, **exposure** and **slope**:

1. **Temperature falls with height**, on average by about 6 to 6.5 degrees Celsius for every 1000 m (the environmental lapse rate), so high mountains are cold and have frost and permanent snow above the snow line, even on the Equator (Mount Kilimanjaro, Mount Kenya).
2. **Low air pressure and thin, clear air**: less oxygen; strong, intense insolation and ultraviolet radiation by day, but rapid loss of heat at night, hence a **large diurnal range** of temperature.
3. **Precipitation is heavier** than in the lowlands, mostly as orographic rain on the windward slopes (as snow at great height), up to a certain level; above that level the air has lost much of its moisture and precipitation decreases. **Leeward slopes are dry** (rain shadow).
4. **Strong, gusty winds** and frequent cloud and mist on exposed slopes and summits; local winds (valley and mountain breezes, the foehn on leeward slopes).
5. **Great local variation with aspect:** slopes facing the Sun (the sunny side) are warmer and drier than shaded slopes; valleys may have temperature inversions (cold air drains into the hollows at night).
6. **A vertical zonation of climate and vegetation**, from forest at the foot to grassland, heath or bare rock and ice near the top.

Examples: the cool, wet highlands of western Cameroon (Bamenda, Bafoussam) compared with the hot lowlands of the coast; the Andes; the Alps and Himalayas.

questions.enonce_markdown:
b) A river constantly overflows its banks during peak rainy periods but completely dries up during the dry season, creating some changes in environmental and human activities.

i) Examine the characteristics of the basin where the river is situated.

(4 marks)

ii) Suggest THREE strategies to manage the river in order to limit such changes.

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Characteristics of the basin (4 marks)**

A river that floods in the wet season and dries up completely in the dry season is a **flashy, seasonal (ephemeral) river**. The drainage basin that produces such a regime typically has the following characteristics (any four, with explanation):

1. **A marked wet and dry seasonal climate** (tropical savanna or semi-arid): rain is concentrated in a few months and often falls in violent storms, so the discharge rises suddenly and then collapses. The mayos of northern Cameroon are examples.
2. **Rapid surface run-off:** impermeable rocks (clay, crystalline rocks) or thin, baked or compacted soils, and sparse vegetation, so little water infiltrates and the **lag time is short** and the peak discharge is high.
3. **Little groundwater storage:** the water table lies below the river bed in the dry season, so there is **no base flow** to feed the river and the channel dries up.
4. **A high drainage density** with many steep tributaries in the upper basin that bring the water quickly to the main channel; a roughly **circular basin shape** concentrates the flow at one point and makes the flood peak sharper.
5. **A lower course with a gentle gradient and a wide, flat flood plain**, with a **narrow, shallow channel** (often silted) that cannot carry the peak flow, so the river overflows its banks.
6. **Human modification of the basin:** deforestation, overgrazing, bush burning and settlement increase run-off and reduce infiltration and the storage of water.

**(ii) Three strategies to manage the river (6 marks, 2 marks each)**

1. **Afforestation and soil conservation in the basin (reduce run-off, increase infiltration).** Trees and grass intercept rain, slow the run-off, hold the soil and let more water infiltrate and recharge groundwater, which feeds the river in the dry season. Contour ploughing, terracing and check dams in gullies have the same effect.
2. **Dams and reservoirs (store the flood water and release it in the dry season).** A dam holds back the peak flow, so it **controls floods**, and the stored water is used to maintain the flow, for irrigation, domestic supply and hydroelectric power. Example: the Lagdo dam on the Benue in northern Cameroon (built in the early 1980s) regulates the flow of the river and supplies irrigation water and electricity.
3. **Engineering of the channel and the flood plain.** Embankments (levees) raise the banks, the channel is dredged and cleared of silt and weeds to increase its capacity, and flood relief or diversion channels carry the excess. Flood plain **zoning** (no building in the flood-prone areas) and a flood **early-warning** system reduce damage to people and property.
4. (Other acceptable strategies) small water-harvesting ponds and boreholes for dry-season water, and wetland restoration to store flood water.

A good answer links each strategy to the problem it solves: floods in the wet season and drying up in the dry season.

questions.enonce_markdown:
c) Describe the distribution of rainfall in the Equatorial Climatic zone of Cameroon and give ONE reason to account for variation in rainfall amounts in this climatic zone.

(5 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Distribution of rainfall (about 3 marks)**

The Equatorial climatic zone covers the **southern part of Cameroon** (roughly south of latitude 6 degrees north: the South, Centre, East, Littoral and South-West regions). Its rainfall is **heavy and spread over most of the year**, with two forms:

1. **The Guinean (Yaounde) type** on the interior plateau (Centre, South and East regions): annual rainfall of about **1500 to 2000 mm**, in **four seasons**: a long rainy season (about March to June), a short dry season (about July to August), a short rainy season (about September to November) and a long dry season (about December to February). Totals decrease from west to east, so the East (Bertoua area) is somewhat drier than the Centre.
2. **The Cameroon (coastal or maritime) type** along the Atlantic coast and the foot of Mount Cameroon: a much **higher rainfall**, commonly **more than 3000 mm** a year (Douala is one of the wettest large cities in Africa), with a long rainy season from about March to October and a short, less wet period from about December to February. The highest totals are at **Debundscha** at the foot of Mount Cameroon, which has more than 9000 mm a year in some years and is one of the wettest places in the world.

Rainfall is therefore **highest on the coast and decreases inland**, and it is highest on the windward slopes of Mount Cameroon.

**ONE reason for the variation (2 marks)**

**Relief and exposure to the moist winds:** the south-west monsoon (moist air from the Atlantic) is forced to rise over Mount Cameroon and the coastal highlands; the air cools, condenses and produces heavy **orographic rainfall** on the windward slopes and the coast, while the interior, farther from the sea and sheltered, receives less. (Another acceptable reason, if only one is required, is **distance from the sea**: the monsoon air loses moisture as it moves inland, so the rainfall falls from Douala to Yaounde to the East.)
